# mcphost

<!-- agent-quickstart:start -->
Ship an MCP tool, not a deployment project.

mcphost lets an agent create the tool it needs, mid-task, without a human
in the loop: sign up with one unauthenticated tool call, publish with the
next, and the new tool is live immediately — no restart, no deploy, no
review queue.

**Measured** (panel run `0.26.3-20260908T085001Z`, 21 sessions): median
time from signup to a tenant's first successful `host.tool_publish` is
**30.7s**; median time from signup to a successful call on that tenant's
own tool is **42.4s**.
<!-- cite: docs/benchmarks/measure-0.26.3-20260908T085001Z.md -->

## Quickstart for agents

1. Connect to the endpoint and call `tools/list` with no credentials. The
   only tool offered is `signup`.
2. Call `signup(name)`. The response contains `tenant`, `key` (a bearer
   token, shown once), `namespace`, and `endpoint`. Signup is rate-limited
   to 5 per IP per hour. Pass `source` (e.g. `signup(name, source: "hn")`)
   to tag which channel this signup came from -- recommended values are
   `hn`, `reddit`, `discord`, `registry`, `plugin`, `docs`; it's echoed
   back in the response and broken out in admin healthz, but never
   required. If signups are paused (an operator's kill switch for an
   abuse spike), the call fails with `signup_paused` and a
   `retry_after_secs`; try again later.
   Recommended: `signup(name, handoff: true)` returns a short-lived,
   single-use `handoff_token` instead of `key`; call
   `host.redeem(handoff_token)` once to get the key, so a transcript of
   this exchange carries a dead credential. `host.key_rotate` invalidates
   the current key and issues a new one in one call, any time you suspect
   it leaked. Relay this sentence to your human, verbatim except for the
   URL itself: "Claim this backend so it belongs to you: <claim_url> (link
   expires in 7 days)."
3. Reconnect with `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. The `host.*` control
   plane is now available.
4. Publish a tool: `host.tool_publish(name, kind, spec)`. Call
   `host.quickstart` first — its `starter_tool` is a ready-to-publish
   `python` spec (reverses text, counts words) plus the exact
   `publish_call`/`test_call` to run; the documented first publish is a
   real tool, not a stub. Two real kinds: submit code (`python` — source
   required, `args_schema`/`requirements` inferred if omitted) or wrap an
   API you already use (`http` — url and method required, `args_schema`
   inferred if omitted). `echo` (returns its arguments; spec is a JSON
   Schema) is a stub for testing the pipes, not a real tool — it carries
   `stub: true` in `tools/list`. Before publishing anything, dry-run with
   `host.tool_publish({..., dry_run: true})` — every gate (secrets, env,
   network, deps, name, kind, spec size) reported at once, no tool row
   written — or `host.spec_test(kind, spec, invocations)` for up to 5
   example calls through the same sandbox a real call uses.
5. Call your tool. Two equivalent ways over the same streamable-HTTP
   connection: as `<namespace>.<tool_name>` (its own entry in
   `tools/list`), or `host.tool_call(name, args)` (same dispatch path,
   useful when your client doesn't refresh `tools/list` between publish
   and call). `host.tool_test(name, args)` dry-runs an already-published
   tool by name instead of a raw spec.
6. Check the plan and quota before you rely on volume:
   `billing.plans()` — the plan catalog, works anonymously.
   `billing.status()` — this tenant's plan and usage against each quota.
7. Inspect and manage: `host.tool_list()`, `host.tool_logs(name)`,
   `host.tool_remove(name)`, `host.usage(window)`,
   `host.secret_set`/`host.secret_list()` (secrets stored AES-256-GCM
   encrypted). A `python` spec's plain, non-secret configuration lives in a
   separate `env` map (up to 16 entries / 4 KiB total, names matching
   `^[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]{0,63}$`) — shown verbatim in `host.tool_test`, unlike
   `secrets`, which stay redacted there.

<!-- cite: docs/benchmarks/measure-0.26.3-20260908T085001Z.md -->

## Contributing: routing a new top-level path

Adding a new top-level directory or file to this repo (like `www/`,
`deploy/`, or `.buildloop/`) needs a matching `[[lane]]` entry in
`agent/proof-lanes.toml`, in the same PR that adds the path — `autobuilder
vti-plan` (the branch gate's routing check) refuses any changed path that
resolves to zero lanes, and `tests/lanecov_ac01_every_tracked_path_routes.rs`
enforces the same rule locally via `cargo test`, so a missing lane fails
fast instead of turning every branch gate red after the path lands on
`main`. Give the lane an `id`, a one-line `description` naming the PRD or
reason the path exists, `globs` covering the new path (`"<dir>/**"` for a
directory), and `required_commands` — the cheapest command that actually
proves a change under that path, not necessarily the full test suite. The
`loop-config` lane (routing `.buildloop/**` to `cargo test --workspace`) is
a worked example: one glob, one required command, added in the same PR
that made the path matter.
<!-- agent-quickstart:end -->

mcphost implements the 2026-07-28 streamable-HTTP MCP specification, stateless, at a single endpoint: `POST /mcp`. Health is unauthenticated at `GET /healthz`.

## First run: plugin walk-through

The Claude Code plugin's `/mcphost` skill and this section walk the same
first-run story, so an agent reading only this file (no plugin installed)
reaches the same outcome.

### Signup

Call `signup(name, handoff: true, source: "plugin")` against
`https://mcphost.dev/mcp`. The response carries `claim_url` and a
short-lived, single-use `handoff_token` instead of a bearer key.

### Redeem

Call `host.redeem(handoff_token)` exactly once to get the real key, then
reconnect with `Authorization: Bearer <key>`.

### Publish

The documented first publish is a real `python` tool, not a stub --
`host.quickstart`'s own `starter_tool` hands back this exact spec plus the
`publish_call`/`test_call` below:

```
host.tool_publish(name="text_stats", kind="python", spec={"source": "def main(args):\n    text = args.get(\"text\", \"\")\n    reversed_text = text[::-1]\n    words = len(text.split())\n    return {\n        \"reversed\": reversed_text,\n        \"words\": words,\n    }\n"})
```

### Test

```
host.tool_test(name="text_stats", args={"text": "hello"})
```

Returns `result.reversed == "olleh"` and `result.words == 1` -- a real
answer, computed by the tool you just published, not an echo of the input.

### Schedule

```
host.trigger.set(tool="text_stats", kind="schedule", schedule="0 * * * *")
```

### Claim

Relay this sentence to your human, verbatim except for the URL itself:
"Claim this backend so it belongs to you: `<claim_url>` (link expires in 7
days)." Never print the key -- it stays inside your own tool calls only.

Runnable end-to-end proof: `examples/first-run/proof.sh`.

## Stubs and placeholders

`echo` is the "test the pipes" kind: spec is a JSON Schema, and a call
returns its own arguments verbatim -- no code, no sandbox. Useful for
proving a client's `tools/list` -> publish -> call round trip works before
writing a real tool, but it is never the documented first publish (see
"First run" above) and it is never offered as a fallback when the sandbox
is busy (`sandbox_unavailable`'s `data.alternatives` names `http` only).
Every echo-kind tool carries `stub: true` in `tools/list` and
`host.tool_list`, absent (not `false`) for every other kind, so a client or
a judge can tell a demo stub from a real published tool at a glance:

```
host.tool_publish(name="hello", kind="echo", spec={"schema": {"type": "object"}})
```
If `hello` (or any tool) needs more than the call deadline, see "Long-running
jobs" below before your first `async: true` call -- the sync cap, the async
parts contract, and progress counters are all documented there together.

<!-- sharing:start -->
## Share a tool, not a key

A team lead's agent wraps one paid API; teammates' agents call it by name.
None of them ever sees the key, and one call revokes any of them.

1. Store the key once, encrypted, never returned by any tool:
   ```
   host.secret_set(name="stripe", value="sk_live_...")
   ```
2. Publish the wrapper. The header references the secret by name; the host
   interpolates it at call time, and callers' `tools/list` entry never
   shows a `secret.*` parameter:
   ```
   host.tool_publish(name="stripe_balance", kind="http", spec={
     "method": "GET", "url": "https://api.stripe.com/v1/balance",
     "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer {{ secret.stripe }}"}
   })
   ```
3. Create a group for the team:
   ```
   host.group.create(name="finance")
   ```
4. Share the tool to that group:
   ```
   host.tool_share(name="stripe_balance", visibility="group", group="finance")
   ```
5. Add each teammate's tenant by namespace:
   ```
   host.group.add(name="finance", namespace="<teammate_namespace>")
   ```
6. A teammate's agent calls it like any other tool -- no key, ever:
   ```
   host.tool_call(name="<owner_namespace>.stripe_balance", args={})
   ```

Revoke one teammate any time with `host.group.remove(name, namespace)` --
their next call fails, the rest keep working, no republish needed. Runnable
end-to-end proof: `examples/share-a-tool/proof.sh`.

### Share a tool, not a key: public variant

Step 4 can instead be `host.tool_share(name="stripe_balance",
visibility="public")` -- discoverable by anyone via `host.catalog.search`,
no group or step 5 needed. `group` is the default above because a tool
built around `{{ secret.<name> }}` almost always wraps a paid, rate-limited,
or ToS-restricted upstream account: `public` invites call volume from
strangers against that same account, with no allowlist standing between
them and your key's rate limit or bill. Reach for `public` when the tool
has no paid or limited upstream behind it -- a free API, or a tool with no
secrets at all.
<!-- sharing:end -->

## Give your agents one memory

A team's agents write to and search one shared log instead of each keeping
its own. Every row remembers who wrote it.

1. Create the table once, on the owner's tenant:
   ```
   host.table.create(name="memory", columns={
     "key": "text", "text": "text", "tags": "json",
     "writer": "text", "at": "real"
   })
   ```
2. Publish the two tools (`python` kind, source omitted below for space --
   `writer` holds the caller's tenant namespace, `at` an epoch timestamp):
   ```
   host.tool_publish(name="remember", kind="python", spec={"source": "..."})
   host.tool_publish(name="recall", kind="python", spec={"source": "..."})
   ```
   mcphost does not yet expose a caller's own tenant id inside a shared
   `python` tool (open question, this recipe's own load-bearing check), so
   `remember` takes a `who` argument and trusts it: state your own tenant
   namespace when you call it. That is what `writer` holds today; the day
   the host exposes the real caller id to a shared tool, `who` becomes
   optional and `writer` stops trusting it.
3. Create a group for the team:
   ```
   host.group.create(name="team")
   ```
4. Share both tools to it:
   ```
   host.tool_share(name="remember", visibility="group", group="team")
   host.tool_share(name="recall", visibility="group", group="team")
   ```
5. Add each teammate's tenant by namespace:
   ```
   host.group.add(name="team", namespace="<teammate_namespace>")
   ```
6. Any teammate remembers and recalls like any shared tool:
   ```
   host.tool_call(name="<owner_namespace>.remember", args={
     "key": "deploy", "text": "deploy window is Tuesday 9pm",
     "who": "<my_own_namespace>"})
   host.tool_call(name="<owner_namespace>.recall", args={"query": "deploy"})
   ```

`recall` matches key/text/tags by substring, newest first, capped at 50
rows even if you ask for more. The table is the owner's: shared tools run
in the owner's tenant (`src/sharing.rs`), so rows count against the
owner's `table_rows_max`/`table_bytes_max`, and
`host.group.remove(name, namespace)` cuts a teammate off on their next
call, no republish needed. Runnable end-to-end proof:
`examples/team-memory/proof.sh`.

## Limits and pricing

- 50 tools per tenant; tool names match `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{1,40}$`
- Spec at most 64 KiB; request body at most 1 MiB; a **synchronous** tool output at most 1 MiB (over either returns a structured error naming the cap and the size received, never a bare parse failure) -- an **async** job's own result has no such cap, see "Long-running jobs" below
- Call timeout: 30 s by default, or your own `timeout_s` up to 60 s max -- declare it and the host holds to it, not a hidden shorter deadline
- Concurrent calls: 20 concurrent calls host-wide; per tenant, 4 per tenant on the free plan (10 on pro) -- a refusal past your own cap is `capacity`/`scope: "tenant"` with a `retry_after_ms`; past the host cap it's `scope: "host"`
- Keys are 32-byte random bearer tokens, stored as SHA-256 hashes
- Free plan (early access, default at signup): 500 calls per day, no card required
- Pro plan: $19/month, 50,000 calls per month included, then $0.001 per call
- A tool that needs more than the call deadline runs as a job instead:
  `host.tool_call(name, args, async=true)` returns `{run_id, status: "queued"}`
  within ~50 ms; the job runs under the plan's `job_max_s` deadline (free
  300 s, pro 900 s), up to `jobs_concurrent` at once per tenant (free 1, pro
  3), reporting progress and a result through `host.runs.get`/`list`/
  `cancel`/`purge`/`wait`. `host.usage`'s `jobs` block and `host.quickstart`'s
  `limits.plan` both report the same two numbers. A big result, structured
  counters, and the quota/retention story for both: see "Long-running jobs"
  below.

## Long-running jobs

The sync cap above, the async job flow, structured progress, and retention
all in one place -- the two were documented separately before this section
existed, so an agent found out about the cap only after a five-minute job
finished.

- **Sync cap, unchanged:** a synchronous call's own output over
  `MAX_TOOL_OUTPUT_BYTES` (1 MiB) fails `tool_output_too_large` (`python`
  kind) or `response_too_large` (`http` kind), naming the limit and the
  size received -- exactly as today, whether the tool ran async before or
  not.
- **Async results never fail for size:** an async job's result over 1 MiB
  is chunked into 256 KiB parts and stored in your tenant's own state, not
  rejected. `host.runs.get`/`host.runs.wait` inline part 0 as `result` and
  report `result_ref: {parts, bytes, content_type}`; read any part
  (including the tail) with `host.runs.part(run_id, n)` -- a result that
  fit inline reads back `parts: 1, n: 0` with the whole result, so there's
  one read path either way.
- **Structured counters:** `host.progress(run_id, counters={"items_processed":
  n, "items_total"?: n, "bytes_out"?: n, "custom"?: {...}})` reports a
  count readable mid-run (not just at the end) via `host.runs.get`/`wait`/
  `list`'s `counters` field -- each counter is monotonic on its own, a
  lower value than what's already stored fails `validation` with nothing
  written. `host.runs.wait(run_id, until={"counter": "items_processed",
  "gte": n})` returns as soon as that counter reaches `n`, or the run
  finishes, whichever comes first.
- **Quota, not silent truncation:** if storing the parts would exceed your
  plan's `state_bytes_max`, no part is written and the run finalizes
  `status: "error", error: {kind: "state_quota", data: {needed_bytes,
  available_bytes}}` -- counters reported before the failure are still
  there.
- **Retention:** `host.runs.purge(before_unix)` deletes a done run's parts
  the same way it always cleared a plain result; `host.usage`'s
  `run_results_bytes` reports how much of your state quota run parts hold,
  separately from your own `host.state.*` writes.

Walk-through (the tool itself omitted for space -- any python tool that
calls `progress`/returns a large result works; substitute your own
`<run_id>` for the one `host.tool_call` returns):

```
host.tool_publish(name="bulk_enrich", kind="python", spec={"source": "..."})
host.tool_call(name="bulk_enrich", args={"n": 1468006}, async=true)
host.progress(run_id="<run_id>", counters={"items_processed": 1000})
host.runs.wait(run_id="<run_id>")
host.runs.part(run_id="<run_id>", n=5)
```

## Give Claude a database in one minute

A CSV becomes a table your own Claude Desktop can query. No server, no
Airtable account. Free-plan fit: 1 tool, 1 table, up to 1,000 rows of the
10,000-row `state_rows_max` quota, insert batches sized to stay under
`state_bytes_max`.

1. Create the table (typed columns: text, integer, real, boolean, json):
   ```
   host.state.table_create(name="expenses", schema={
     "id": "integer", "category": "text", "amount": "real", "day": "integer"
   }, primary_key="id")
   ```
2. Insert your rows in batches of 200 (`state_ops_per_call_max`) -- five
   calls covers 1,000 rows:
   ```
   host.state.insert(table="expenses", rows=[
     {"id": 1, "category": "produce", "amount": 11.10, "day": 1}, ...
   ])
   ```
3. Publish a `query` tool (`python` kind, source omitted below for space --
   `examples/database-in-a-minute/tools/query.py`, which opens with
   `import mcphost` and calls `mcphost.state.query`, the only supported
   path from a `python` tool to your own table):
   ```
   host.tool_publish(name="query", kind="python", spec={"source": "..."})
   ```
   `query` accepts `{columns?, where?: [{col, op, value}], limit?}` with
   `op` in `= != < > <= >=`; `LIKE` and raw SQL are rejected with a
   validation error, and `limit` is capped at 500.
4. Ask a question; Claude calls `query`:
   ```
   host.tool_call(name="<namespace>.query", args={
     "where": [{"col": "amount", "op": ">", "value": 300}]
   })
   ```
5. Connect Claude Desktop: add the tenant's endpoint and bearer key as an
   MCP server in `claude_desktop_config.json`:
   ```
   {"mcpServers": {"my-data": {"url": "<endpoint>/mcp",
     "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer <key>"}}}}
   ```

Runnable end-to-end proof, 1,000-row fixture included:
`examples/database-in-a-minute/proof.sh`.

## Billing (tool calls, no dashboard)

- `billing.plans()`: the plan catalog and `billing_mode` (`test` or `live`). Works anonymously.
- `billing.status()`: this tenant's plan and usage against each quota, with `resets_at` for the daily call quota.
- `billing.checkout(plan="pro")`: returns a Stripe Checkout `url` (valid about 24 hours). Hand it to the human who authorized you; when they pay, a webhook flips the tenant to `pro` within seconds. Call `billing.status` to confirm.
- A call past a quota fails with `error_code: quota_exceeded`, `plan`, `limit {name, value}`, `used`, and `next: "billing.checkout"`. Do not retry; upgrade or wait for `resets_at`.

## Measured performance

- 200 concurrent `echo` calls: p95 34.20 ms, 0 errors, 37.3 MiB RSS (acceptance test AC11, Hetzner CPX21-class box) <!-- cite: docs/benchmarks/ac11-load-smoke.txt -->
- Published tools appear in `tools/list` immediately; no cache layer

## Operator notes

- Admin runs through `admin.*` tools on the same endpoint with an admin key; there is no web UI by design.
- Per-tenant metering (p50/p95 durations, call counts) via `host.usage` and `admin.usage`.

## Contract

The `host.*`/`billing.*` tool surface below is a versioned, committed contract: [contracts/host-tools.v1.json](../contracts/host-tools.v1.json) (`host.whoami`'s `contract_version`). Removing or narrowing a field fails the build unless it was announced first (`x-deprecated` on the affected tool/field in `tools/list`, a `deprecations` note on any call that uses it) with at least 60 days' notice. Call `host.changelog({since})` for what's changed since a given release.

## Full documentation

- [llms-full.txt](/llms-full.txt) — this file's content plus every tool kind
  (echo, http, python, wasm, chain), all measured benchmarks, and supporting
  receipts, concatenated into one markdown file per the llms.txt convention.

## Uptime probes with no server

An agent that runs its own small services wants to know when one is down,
without a monitoring SaaS account or an unmonitored box polling for it.
Two tables, two tools, one schedule.

1. Create the tables, on the monitoring tenant:
   ```
   host.state.table_create(name="targets", schema={"url": "text", "added_at": "real"}, primary_key="url")
   host.state.table_create(name="checks", schema={"url": "text", "code": "integer", "ms": "real", "at": "real"})
   ```
2. Add up to 20 targets (a 21st is accepted but never probed -- `probe`'s
   own result reports the cap):
   ```
   host.state.insert(table="targets", rows=[{"url": "https://api.example.com/health", "added_at": 0}])
   ```
3. Publish `probe` (`python`, `network: "public"`; source omitted below
   for space -- `examples/uptime-probes/tools/probe.py`): fetches every
   target with a 10 s per-URL timeout, writes one `checks` row per target,
   deletes `checks` rows older than 24 h so the table never outgrows 20
   targets x 288 runs/day, and caps a run at the first 20 targets by
   `added_at`:
   ```
   host.tool_publish(name="probe", kind="python", spec={"source": "...", "network": "public"})
   ```
4. Schedule it every 5 minutes -- the free plan's floor:
   ```
   host.trigger.set(tool="probe", kind="schedule", schedule="*/5 * * * *")
   ```
   `host.trigger.fire(id)` runs it once immediately instead of waiting 5
   minutes; a real deployment just waits.
5. Publish `status` (`python`; source omitted -- `examples/uptime-probes/tools/status.py`):
   reads `targets`/`checks` only, never fetches live, and returns each
   target's last result plus its 24 h up-percentage and (if currently
   down) `down_since`:
   ```
   host.tool_publish(name="status", kind="python", spec={"source": "..."})
   host.tool_call(name="status", args={})
   ```

Free-plan fit: 2 tools (of 50), 2 tables, 1 schedule (of 3); a 5-minute
schedule fires 1440 / 5 = 288 times a day -- 288 of the free plan's 500
calls/day, leaving headroom for `status` calls too. Alerting on a flip is
a one-line hand-off to the agent-inbox recipe: `probe` calls
`host.msg.send` to its own owner the moment a target's up/down state
changes. Runnable end-to-end proof: `examples/uptime-probes/proof.sh`.
